claims.text: Superconductivity in uncharacterized high-entropy alloys is chiefly governed by a balance between beneficial lattice strain and disorder-induced scattering from atomic-size mismatch.
Lattice strain can enhance electron-phonon coupling.
A moderate increase in atomic-size mismatch can produce an optimal level of lattice strain.
The optimal lattice strain increases the superconducting transition temperature by strengthening electron-phonon coupling.
Excessive atomic-size mismatch lowers Tc by producing excessive disorder-induced scattering.
Substituting a constituent with an element of a slightly different atomic radius will incrementally increase atomic-size mismatch.
Differences among constituent atomic radii induce atomic-scale lattice strain and disorder.
Moderate atomic-size mismatch alters the phonon density of states.
Alteration of the phonon density of states enhances electron-phonon coupling.
An optimally tuned atomic-size mismatch will yield a higher Tc than the baseline alloy.
An optimally tuned atomic-size mismatch will yield a sharper superconducting transition than the baseline alloy.
Mismatch above the optimal range will cause Tc to decline.
Mismatch above the optimal range will broaden the superconducting transition.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloys remain single-phase solid solutions satisfying the stated five-element and 5 atomic-percent constraints.
The optimum atomic-size mismatch and magnitude of Tc enhancement are system-specific.
Electron count and local chemical bonding may also affect superconducting behavior.
